progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C1 (dynamic equilibrium needs a closed system; equal rates; a finished reaction is static), C2 (reversible reactions approach equilibrium), C3 (adding a reactant shifts right and deepens the iron thiocyanate red; removing one shifts left; heating favours the reaction that takes in heat; the cobalt solution is pink cold, blue hot, purple at room temperature; Le Chatelier's principle), C4a (sealed NO2 syringe and tubes), and Year 11 Working Scientifically (an independent variable is changed, a dependent variable is measured, controlled variables are kept the same; a risk assessment lists hazards and controls). The words validity, reliability and accuracy are given a plain meaning here even if met in Year 11.
progression.startsWith: Choose a reversible system and compare controlled disturbances. The video opens: This tube of iron thiocyanate has sat at the same pale red for an hour. Is that proof that it's an equilibrium, with both reactions still running?
progression.stopsAfter: stating the reversibility test (change, then reverse the change; a return is the evidence) and the magnesium contrast; stating whether a set-up is open or closed and why an equilibrium test needs a closed one; planning the six-tube disturbance investigation with a reference tube, one change per tube, side-by-side judging and a dilution control; naming the independent, dependent and controlled variables; predicting the results and giving the C3 reason in a clause; defining validity, reliability and accuracy for this investigation; writing a risk assessment row (hazard, harm, control) for the real hazards. No K, no Q, no colourimeter data (P02), no conduct.
progression.nextLesson: putting a number on where an equilibrium sits (route chem-m5-c05), without naming K (C3 and C4b convention).

teaching.task: How do you show in the lab that a reaction is reversible, and that an equilibrium really responds to a disturbance, with evidence you can trust?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) an unchanged appearance cannot tell a running equilibrium from a finished reaction, so evidence needs a push (1); (2) the reversibility test: change, then reverse the change; one change proves nothing, a return does (2); (3) burning magnesium does not come back under any school conditions, so it is treated as irreversible; the hydrate test was open, so it shows reversibility, not an equilibrium (3); (4) an equilibrium investigation needs a closed system, and the method must say what is sealed (4); (5) a pale stock, an untouched reference and one change per tube, judged side by side (5); (6) independent, dependent and controlled variables (6); (7) expected results with the C3 reason in a clause (7); (8) adding a solution dilutes, so a paler tube is not yet evidence; the dilution control separates a shift from dilution (8); (9) temperature in a sealed tube, with the return to room temperature as a second reversibility check (9); (10) validity, reliability, accuracy (10); (11) risk assessment (11); memory aids (12); two attempts with brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two investigations, one question each. (A) Is it reversible? Push it one way, then reverse the change and see whether the start comes back (cobalt hydrate), against an irreversible contrast (burning magnesium). (B) How does an equilibrium respond to a disturbance, and how do you know the change is real? Reference tube, one change per tube, side-by-side judging, the dilution control, temperature in a sealed tube. Then validity, reliability and accuracy in plain words, the risk assessment, and two classic exam questions.
teaching.openingDecision: To show that a reaction can run both ways, and that it responds to a change, you have to push it and watch what happens. So how do you plan an investigation with evidence you can trust?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) a tube made paler by ten drops of silver nitrate solution, concluded "shifted left": what extra tube makes the conclusion valid, and why? Answer: an identical tube with ten drops of water (dilution control). Crossed mistake: "repeat it three times" (that improves reliability, not validity). (A2) heated pink cobalt chloride crystals turn blue, concluded "reversible": evaluate. Answer: one direction only; add water to the cooled blue solid and see pink return; the open tube shows reversibility, not an equilibrium. Crossed mistake: "correct, the colour changed".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, p49 to p50): C5-IQ1-01 "conduct practical investigations to analyse the reversibility of chemical reactions, for example: cobalt(II) chloride hydrated and dehydrated; iron(III) nitrate and potassium thiocyanate; burning magnesium; burning steel wool (ACSCH090)"; C5-IQ2-01 "investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier's principle can be used to predict such effects, for example: heating cobalt(II) chloride hydrate; interaction between nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide; iron(III) thiocyanate and varying concentration of ions (ACSCH095)". This video prepares students to plan, record and analyse the investigation and does not claim to replace conducting it.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, three constant zones (short question top left, apparatus centre, one current card in the right third). Colour key: Fe3+ pale yellow, SCN- grey, FeSCN2+ red, cobalt pink and blue ions, reference tube marked with a teal tag, controls teal, hazards terracotta, risk controls green. Reuse and new items: the C3 painted iron tubes (`c3-iron-tube-start-v1.png`, `c3-iron-tube-deep-v1.png`), the C3 cobalt tubes in water-bath beakers (`c3-cobalt-tube-pink-v1.png`, `-purple-`, `-blue-`), the C9 sealed NO2 tubes (`c9-no2-tube-brown-v1.png`, `c9-no2-tube-pale-v1.png`), the C4a syringe parts (`c4a-syringe-barrel-v1.png`, `c4a-syringe-plunger-v1.png`, screen tag only), `m6-white-tile-v1.png`, `m5x-bottle-fe-v1.png` and `m5x-bottle-scn-v1.png` (reagent bottles, coded labels on the blank labels), `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png` (distilled water), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (bath, coded water fill), `c8-thermometer-hot-v1.png`, `c9-ice-cube-v1.png`, the C3 equation chip style and shift arrows, the countdown ring, the key notes board. New coded items: the "push it, bring it back" arrow loop, the six-tube comparison bar (swatches against the reference), the variables card, the expected results table, the risk assessment table (hazard, harm, control), the validity / reliability / accuracy cards, the open/closed boundary outline (dashed line around the tube showing what can cross). New painted plates are listed in the Codex asset brief.
design.transitionPlan: The still iron tube and the question open the lesson; the cobalt crystal tube replaces it for the push-and-return loop; the magnesium ribbon and ash plate give the contrast and the open tube returns with a dashed outline; three sealed-or-open boundary plates follow; the six-tube row slides onto the white tile and stays while the variables, expected results and dilution control cards take the right third one at a time; the cobalt bath tube replaces the row for temperature; the validity, risk and aid cards follow; the attempt boards clear the screen and the feedback rebuilds the loop and the tube comparison bar; the plan card and the six-tube row return for the handoff; scene crossfade with settle.
